target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and safety.
objection: Those benefits are often outweighed by harms: AI can replace workers and depress wages, weaken students’ and adults’ critical thinking by encouraging answer-copying, reproduce or intensify racial discrimination, and create serious privacy and surveillance risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not good for society because of job loss, weaker learning, bias, and privacy harms.
objection: Those risks do not show AI is inherently harmful; they show AI must be governed. AI can augment workers, act as a scaffolded tutor, be audited for fairness, and be made privacy-preserving with techniques like data minimization and on-device processing, so the harms are manageable rather than decisive.

target: AG1’s assumption that governance, audits, education guardrails, and privacy-preserving techniques are reliable enough to make AI good for society.
objection: The proposed fixes are too costly, too slow, and too hard to guarantee at scale because incentives favor speed and profit, oversight lags deployment, many systems are opaque, and “privacy-preserving” tools still leave meaningful exposure and failure modes.

target: AG2’s assumption that because safeguards are imperfect, AI cannot be considered good for society.
objection: AI does not need perfect governance to be net beneficial because it replaces imperfect human systems that already have bias, privacy, and safety problems; with staged deployment, monitoring, and regulation, AI can still improve outcomes relative to current baselines.

target: AG1’s claim that audits, monitoring, rollback, and human review can reliably control AI harms.
objection: Audit trails do not equal real accountability, AI can scale and accelerate human biases, and education/privacy guardrails are easily gamed by incentives, user workarounds, and the power asymmetry between ordinary people and large platforms.

target: AG2’s claim that monitoring, audit trails, and human review are too weak to make AI good for society.
objection: Monitoring can be privacy-preserving rather than surveillance-heavy; rollback and pre-deployment testing can stop failures before broad deployment; human review can be structured with sampling and escalation; and accessibility benefits are still real even when some data processing is involved.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring, testing, and human review can keep AI harms under control.
objection: Privacy-preserving monitoring still requires more data and can itself become surveillance; pre-deployment tests miss real-world edge cases; human review can become rubber-stamping under volume pressures; and accessibility tools still involve the same core privacy/bias infrastructure.

target: AG2’s claim that monitoring and oversight necessarily worsen privacy and fail to prevent bias or harm.
objection: Monitoring can be designed with aggregate metrics, short retention, access controls, on-device evaluation, and differential privacy; staged rollout plus evaluation can prevent harms before broad deployment; and human review can be risk-based rather than a rubber stamp, while accessibility tools still deliver major social benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring and staged rollout solve the privacy/accountability problem.
objection: Privacy-preserving monitoring either becomes too weak to detect discrimination or requires more data and recreates the privacy problem; pre-deployment tests miss edge cases and future drift; proprietary systems make oversight performative; and incentives toward speed and scale still dominate outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that incentives and opacity make AI governance ineffective and therefore AI not good for society.
objection: Society can change incentives directly with mandatory procurement standards, independent evaluations, and liability; opaque systems can still be held accountable through independent behavioral audits and standardized reporting; the right comparison is not perfection but better outcomes than current human systems.

target: AG1’s claim that liability, audits, procurement rules, and risk-tiering can make AI good for society.
objection: Those governance tools do not scale across consumer apps, small businesses, and third-party integrations; audits are limited by vendor control and sampling; risk-tiering can be gamed by under-classifying danger; and scalable automation can still amplify bias, privacy invasion, and economic displacement.

target: AG2’s claim that governance failures mean AI is not good for society.
objection: AI’s real benefits are already concentrated in lower-stakes domains like accessibility, health, and safety, and governance can be operationalized with version-locked deployments, provenance, and measurable requirements; imperfect safeguards can still yield net social improvement.

target: AG1’s claim that lower-stakes AI can be separated from harmful uses and that restricting AI broadly would be too blunt.
objection: In real deployment, beneficial and harmful uses are entangled: low-stakes tools still create the same privacy and bias infrastructure, spill over into higher-stakes systems, and redistribute harms disproportionately to workers and racial minorities, so broad restriction is safer.

target: AG2’s claim that beneficial and harmful AI uses are inevitably entangled.
objection: Purpose limitation, compartmentalized pipelines, and enforceable restrictions can separate low-risk from high-risk uses; disparate-impact testing can address distributional harms; and blanket restriction would sacrifice real accessibility and safety gains.

target: AG1’s claim that purpose limitation and compartmentalization can prevent spillover.
objection: Those controls are hard to enforce because data is centralized in multi-tenant systems, integrations with analytics/ad/fraud tools create spillover, vendors have incentives to repurpose data, and impact testing can only detect harm after people are already affected.

target: AG2’s claim that any imperfection in controls means AI should be broadly restricted.
objection: Separation can be enforced end-to-end for the specific use cases that matter most through risk-tiering, on-device or hybrid architectures, and contract-based compliance; AI should be treated as a portfolio of different risk levels rather than a single harmful monolith.

target: AG1’s claim that low-risk accessibility/health AI can be safely isolated.
objection: Even helpful AI creates vendor lock-in, centralized control, residual privacy risk, and incentive-driven risk classification; on-device processing still leaves telemetry and metadata risks; and the whole ecosystem’s harms can make society worse overall even if some users benefit.

target: AG2’s claim that centralized control and lock-in are inevitable in beneficial AI.
objection: Interoperability, portability, local/user-controlled modes, and accessibility-first standards can reduce lock-in and centralized control; because net good only requires measurable improvement, not perfection, AI can still be good for society with enforceable protections.

target: AG1’s claim that portability, user settings, and accessibility standards can meaningfully limit harm.
objection: Portability does not port the proprietary model behavior that creates the benefit, user privacy settings are often cosmetic or overridden by defaults and updates, and accessibility improvements do not stop spillover into labor displacement, biased decisions, or degraded critical thinking.

target: AG2’s claim that user settings and portability are insufficient, so AI should not be broadly promoted.
objection: Stronger mechanisms like independent certification, continuous compliance, integration-level restrictions, separate model instances for different risk tiers, and outcome-based reporting can make controls real and prevent spillover without banning AI.

target: AG1’s claim that certification and continuous compliance can make AI reliably good for society.
objection: Certification cannot keep pace with frequent model updates and vendor changes, audits often certify paperwork rather than real downstream outcomes, incentives encourage strategic compliance, and even “certified” accessibility AI can still misrecognize accents or contribute to labor displacement and surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that operational safeguards cannot keep up with AI deployment.
objection: Operational safeguards can be made concrete with signed model versions, locked deployment pipelines, provenance tracking, real liability, and accessibility/education-specific evaluation, so AI can still be good for society when governance is operational rather than merely reputational.

target: AG1’s claim that operational safeguards can reliably prevent AI harms.
objection: Those safeguards require more surveillance and trace data, do not scale across the broader consumer and small-business ecosystem, and still cannot prevent irreversible discrimination, lost opportunities, or answer-substitution harms before they occur; therefore AI is not reliably good for society.

target: AG2’s conclusion that AI should be broadly restricted because operational safeguards are hard to scale.
objection: Broad restriction would impose large opportunity costs by reducing real accessibility and health benefits now, AI can prevent harm in workplace safety and health contexts before accidents occur, and governance can be selective rather than all-or-nothing by targeting high-risk uses while allowing lower-risk beneficial ones.
